title: Introduction to Binary Tree
description: Understand what a binary tree is, how nodes are connected, and common tree terminology

7. What to Know Before Solving Problems

blocks.text: As computers started handling large amounts of data, searching through a simple list became slow and inefficient. Computer scientists needed a way to organize data so that items could be found, inserted, and deleted more quickly. By dividing data into smaller left and right groups repeatedly, they created the concept of a binary tree. This structure greatly improved the efficiency of many operations and became a fundamental data structure in computer science.
1. What Is Binary Tree

A Binary Tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children called the left child and right child. It's one of the most fundamental structures in computer science, used everywhere from file systems to databases to compilers.
Unlike arrays or linked lists (which are linear), a binary tree is non-linear. Data is organised in levels, branching downward from a single starting point called the root.
Think of it like a family tree: one ancestor at the top, each person can have up to two direct descendants, and it keeps branching until you reach people with no children (leaf nodes).

items: Root: The root is the topmost node of a tree. It is the starting point of the entire tree and does not have any parent node. Every tree has exactly one root.
Node: A node is an individual element in a tree. It stores data and may have links to one or more child nodes.
Parent: A parent is a node that has one or more children directly below it. Every node except the root has exactly one parent.
Child: A child is a node that is directly connected below another node. The node above it is called its parent.
Leaf Node: A leaf node is a node that has no children. It represents the end of a branch in the tree.
Height: The height of a node is the number of edges in the longest path from that node down to a leaf node. A leaf node has a height of 0.
Depth: The depth of a node is the number of edges from the root to that node. The root node has a depth of 0.
Level: A level contains all nodes that are at the same depth. The root is usually considered to be at level 0.
Subtree: A subtree is a smaller tree formed by any node and all of its descendants. Every node in a tree can be considered the root of its own subtree.
Ancestors: Ancestors are all the nodes on the path from a given node back to the root. This includes the node's parent, grandparent, and so on up to the root.
Siblings: Siblings are nodes that share the same parent. They exist at the same level of the tree and are directly related through their parent.

blocks.text: Each node in a binary tree stores three things: the data, a pointer to its left child, and a pointer to its right child. If a child doesn't exist, that pointer is null.

blocks.text: Understanding the types is crucial many problems constrain which type they use, and different types enable different algorithmic guarantees.

items: Full Binary Tree: Every node has either 0 or 2 children. No node has exactly one child.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are completely filled except possibly the last level, which is filled from left to right.
Perfect Binary Tree: Every internal node has 2 children, and all leaf nodes are at the same level.
Balanced Binary Tree: For every node, the height difference between the left and right subtrees is at most1. This keeps operations efficient.
Binary Search Tree (BST): A tree where left child < parent < right child. This allows fast searching, insertion, and deletion.
Degenerate (Skewed) Tree: Every node has onlyone child, making the tree look like a linked list. This is the least efficient tree structure.

blocks.text: Traversal means visiting every node exactly once. Unlike arrays (only one way), trees have multiple traversal strategies and choosing the right one is key to solving problems efficiently.
1. Depth-First Search (DFS)

Depth-First Search (DFS) is a traversal technique where we explore one path as deeply as possible before backtracking and exploring other paths. The three main DFS traversals are Inorder, Preorder, and Postorder.
1. Inorder Traversal (Left → Root → Right):
Inorder first visits the left subtree, then the current node, and finally the right subtree. In a Binary Search Tree (BST), this traversal visits nodes in sorted order.
2. Preorder Traversal (Root → Left → Right)
Preorder visits the current node first, then the left subtree, and finally the right subtree. It is useful when you need to process a node before its children.
3. Postorder Traversal (Left → Right → Root)
Postorder visits both subtrees before visiting the current node. It is commonly used when deleting a tree or processing children before their parent.
2. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

Breadth-First Search (BFS) is a traversal technique that visits nodes level by level, starting from the root and moving downward. Instead of going deep into one branch, it explores all nodes at the current level before moving to the next level.
1. Level Order Traversal (BFS)
Level Order visits nodes level by level, starting from the root and moving downward. It uses a queue to keep track of nodes that need to be visited next.
2. Uses a Queue & Visits Level by Level
Instead of exploring one branch deeply, BFS visits nodes level by level, starting from the root. It first processes all nodes at Level 0, then all nodes at Level 1, followed by Level 2, and so on.
To keep track of which node should be visited next, BFS uses a queue, which follows the FIFO (First In, First Out)principle. Nodes are added to the back of the queue and removed from the front.
This ensures that all nodes at the current level are processed before moving to the next level, making BFS the natural choice when a problem asks for level-by-level traversal of a tree.
These come up directly in interview questions. Memorise them.

items: Maximum Nodes in a Binary Tree: A binary tree of height h can have at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes. This happens when every level of the tree is completely filled.

Height of a Perfect Binary Tree: A perfect binary tree with n nodes has a height of log₂(n + 1) - 1. Since every level is completely filled, the height grows very slowly compared to the number of nodes.
Minimum Height for n Nodes:A binary tree with n nodes can have a minimum height of ⌊log₂(n)⌋. This occurs when the tree is perfectly balanced.
Leaf Nodes in a Full Binary Tree: In a full binary tree, the number of leaf nodes is always one greater than the number of internal nodes.
Array Representation of a Complete Binary Tree: When a complete binary tree is stored in an array, the left child of a node at index i is located at 2i + 1, and the right child is located at 2i + 2.
Maximum Nodes at a Level: The maximum number of nodes that can exist at level l is 2^l. Each level can contain at most twice as many nodes as the previous level.
File Systems: File systems use a tree structure to organize data. The root represents the main drive, folders act as branches, and files are stored as leaf nodes.
Expression Trees: Compilers use expression trees to represent and evaluate mathematical expressions. Each operator becomes a node, while operands become its children.
Heaps: Heaps are complete binary trees used to implement priority queues. They are commonly used in algorithms like Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm.
Decision Trees: Decision trees are used in machine learning to make predictions and classifications. Each node represents a decision, and each branch represents a possible outcome.
Database Indexing: Databases use B-Trees and their variants to store indexes efficiently. This allows fast searching, insertion, and deletion of records.
Huffman Coding: Huffman Coding uses binary trees to create optimal prefix codes for data compression. It is widely used in formats such as ZIP and JPEG to reduce file size.

content.title: 7. What to Know Before Solving Problems

blocks.text: After reading this, make sure you can confidently answer these before jumping to problems:

items: Can you write the TreeNode class from scratch in your preferred language?
Do you know the difference between height and depth of a node?
Can you identify if a tree is full, complete, perfect, or balanced just by looking at it?
Can you trace inorder, preorder, and postorder traversal by hand on a small tree?
Do you know when to use DFS vs BFS for tree problems?
Can you implement traversal both recursively and iteratively?

blocks.text: The upcoming chapters (Level Order, Preorder, Inorder, Postorder, Advanced) each deep-dive one traversal type with problems, patterns, and edge cases. This intro chapter is your foundation.
